title: Ask HN: How to measure the energy impact of a website in Linux
text:
For the context, I'm on Fedora Kinoite (Atomic KDE) 44. The laptop is an AMD Frame.work 13.

Today I noticed that Firefox is showing a speaker icon all the time. Closing my pinned tans one by one showed that it's because of ChatGPT.

Now I had this question: does it really impact my battery life?

I can't rely only on the CPU energy. Maybe keeping an Audio pathway causes other hardware components to be unnecessarily active.

One way I could think of is to run on battery, and compare how fast it discharges with and without the tab open.

Are there other ways to reliably measure energy usage and narrow it down to individual processes/tabs?

title: Show HN: Overboard – Mac agent orchestrator with ship captains that spawn agents
text:
Hi HN, I’m Mark. Companies are really pushing cloud agents, but I found myself wanting to run agents on my Mac off-hours on my existing Claude/Codex subs.

I'd hit my usage limit coding with Fable, but not my limit on other models for tasks like marketing, research and content creation. So I built an orchestrator that organizes my agents into departments (or ships) where they have overriding goals/milestones and a "captain" agent can spawn other agents working in that department.

I think this structure works better than individual agent workers in an office. (Mundler Difflin)

The user can prompt the agent dispatcher for one-off or recurring tasks, which can be controlled from a Slack or a Telegram bot. Since Overboard has context about all your local projects it knows where it should spawn an agent. You can also talk to department heads or the main agent to see what human blockers are stalling projects, or give new direction for a department. Would love to hear feedback about the project. It's not open-source but there is a 14 day trial so anyone can test if it's useful before buying a license. (one-time $49)

title: Re: Gemini Replaces Google Assistant on Android...
text:
Spent most of the day trying to figure out why my phone can no longer control my Google Home - no automations, no routines, "Hey Google" doesn't work anymore. Turns out Google just binned the Assistant and forced Gemini.

Except Gemini doesn't work. Can't do automations. Won't respond to voice activation. Even if I button push it and ask it to run the automations, it just searches the web and explains how to set up new ones.

Absolutely infuriating - breaking a product that's worked for years for 'AI'.

I think Gemini's own response to me explains it best:

"It comes down to a fundamental difference in how the two systems were built, and Google rushing the transition before the new platform was actually feature-complete.

It really is an absolute mess, and you shouldn't have to jump through technical hoops just to fix basic phone functions that worked fine yesterday."

title: Show HN: Ciao – Control coding agents from your phone
text:
Hi HN, I built Ciao to solve problems I was experiencing:

1. Connecting to a new host should be as seamless as possible. I SSH a lot nowadays, and I find the key sharing across devices cumbersome.

2. I get annoyed by setting up insert-your-favorite VPN on new machines. They're all great. I don't want to think about them.

3. There's a lot of harnesses: Claude Code and Codex now have decent mobile push notifications but what about Pi or xyz-shiny-new harness? The harness is another tool that should be abstracted out.

4. I want a single application that has the big picture of all of my agents. Tmux and Herdr are great but they don't have an overview of all my connected machines' agents.

---

With Ciao you curl|sh the daemon --> run ciao pair --> point your phone's camera at the QR code --> and you're connected. It uses iroh for accountless and E2EE connection. There's an optional relay server for APNS which too is E2EE.

One of my favorite aspects of agentic-engineering is being able to just have a lot of fun with programming. Among many features, I built a visually pleasing toggle between terminal-mode and native-chat-mode. If you install Ciao, come back here and tell me what you think.

---

Full transparency: this is a repost from yesterday, it was a massive day in AI.

title: Re: Claude Says...
text:
It took maybe a decade to teach people to not use "@here" on Slack, and avg. response time of an email isn't 10 minutes. Technology comes out, many people fumble through for years, until finally some etiquette is formed. Happens all the time.

I don't remember the last time someone dropped me the first link out of a Google search, telling me they haven't read themselves and have no idea about its contents. Yet I see it happen in various 1-1 and public settings with Claude all the time.

In those discussions people often don't use this as a "Here let me Claude it for you" kind of protest, but genuinely they mean "I copy pasted this topic to Claude, and Claude said this. I'm meat-proxying to you, and absolutely haven't invested a single microsecond of my time on it". Obviously the expectation is you'd invest the effort they haven't.

My strategy and hope, is to give it a decade. It will probably get better.

title: Show HN: Open-source model routing for coding agents at Astra-level performance
text:
A few months ago we started building a model router for coding agents because we thought we could outperform any single model with an ensemble approach. Recently we’ve achieved that milestone and I want to talk about how we did it.

First of all, a quick explanation: the Weave Router (https://github.com/weave-os/router) plugs into any coding agent (e.g. Claude Code or Codex) and intelligently switches between LLMs. So, for example, Astra handles tricky debugging or complex system design tasks, and Deepseek v4 Flash handles simple frontend updates.

What we’re announcing today is our new routing model, which we’re calling Weave Router 2.0. We benchmarked 2.0 against GPT-6 Astra on Terminal Bench 4.0 and SWE Atlas. On both benchmarks, the router had equivalent pass rates. On Terminal Bench, the router hit 52% of Astra’s cost, and completed tasks 2.2x faster. On SWE Atlas, the router cost 54% as much as Astra and ran 2.5x faster. (Full results on our website at https://weaveos.com/router!)

It turns out training a model to route effectively - taking into consideration model capabilities, costs, cache awareness, and more - is a really hard problem! I want to talk about three ways we were able to improve so much over the last few months: 1) a new architecture, 2) larger training data set size, and 3) smarter cache-eviction impact calculation.

1) a new architecture. Our initial approach used an RL model without many priors. While RL is still an important part of the story, the cost of fully exploring the space of routing decisions is very high, so we’ve taken some shortcuts that have significantly improved performance. In particular: we trained a hidden Markov model to trace the session state, then a classifier maps the session to one of a few buckets of similar models. This significantly shrinks the space to explore, by throwing out most models that could not reasonably serve the given session. This rearchitecture was the single biggest performance unlock!

Consider how large the search space for the routing problem is. Take a typical coding agent session, with ~100 agent turns (i.e. 100 LLM API calls). Technically there are 100 chances to select a model. If we assume a roster of ~10 models (of course there are lots more but we can remove any that are Pareto dominated), then there are 10^100 possible paths through that session. We simply cannot explore all of them! So that's why clever tricks to shrink this space are so important.

2) larger training data set size (much less technically interesting but still an important part of the story). By using frontier LLMs to help us label a larger and more diverse set of coding agent sessions, we were able to bootstrap the two models discussed in 1) to a better state, while also providing even richer reward signals for RL.

3) smarter cache-eviction impact calculation. One of the hardest parts of routing well (if you care about saving money) is using the model caches intelligently. We built a subsystem that can calculate the expected value of switching models (and thus paying a high one-time cost to fill up a different cache) much more accurately, helping us avoid costly and unnecessary switches in more cases, while still switching when the benefit outweighs the cost. This is where most of our improvement on cost has come from.

We still have a lot of room to continue to improve (we won’t rest until we’re consistently beating Astra/Fable, not just tying!) but matching frontier model performance was a huge milestone for our routing model, and in my opinion validates our initial hypothesis that an ensemble of models can do better than any single model ever could.

Our router is open source (https://github.com/weave-os/router) so anyone can try it out. Or if you prefer you can use our hosted version (https://weaveos.com/router).

title: Show HN: Beyond "chat with your database" – agentic data exploration
text:
Business intelligence is changing. AI can now do more than turn a question into a single SQL query: it can investigate a question through a series of queries, examining the result of one query to decide what to query next.

Today, to answer a business question against a database, analysts use a tool like Tableau: they select relevant data, build an initial view using fields, filters, calculations, and visualizations, then look for patterns or anomalies. They form hypotheses and test them — filtering by region, drilling into customer cohorts, comparing time periods, or creating calculations to validate or rule out an explanation. They repeat this process until the evidence supports an answer, then save a workbook or dashboard for others to review and monitor.

With a single question, AI can now perform much of this exploratory loop: it can investigate the data, follow the evidence through multiple queries, and present the supporting analysis. This is agentic data analysis — AI autonomously decides what to investigate next based on the results it has already found.

Reportr puts agentic AI at the center of the experience, then builds complementary capabilities around it to address AI's limitations:

SEMANTIC LAYER

Production databases are rarely clean: columns that are no longer used, cryptic names like status2, misc, or flag, columns whose meaning has quietly shifted over time, tables that linger long after their purpose is gone, and so on. This is known as schema rot. AI tools guess wrong against schemas like this. Reportr's semantic layer lets you give tables and columns business-friendly names and descriptions, document relationships, capture business rules, and flag what AI should ignore — so it's working from what your data means, not just what it's called.

USER OVERSIGHT

AI-generated answers can be wrong. Reportr lets you inspect the SQL executed to arrive at an answer. It also provides explanations of what the SQL does (understandable by business users), and how it works (intended for technical users). You can review the analysis rather than simply accepting AI's conclusions.

BETTER USER EXPERIENCE

Reportr UI is specifically optimized for chatting with a database. Database queries often return large number of records. Ask which customers haven't placed an order in the last 90 days, and the answer is a list of customers. Reportr displays tabular data in an interactive grid that can handle thousand of records without breaking a sweat. The grid supports sorting, searching, and filtering.

REPORTS AND DASHBOARDS

Chat is ephemeral. Every conversation starts fresh, and that's fine for exploration — but not for information you need every week. When a chart or table reveals something worth tracking, save it as a report. Combine reports into dashboards to monitor changes over time, share findings, and keep important insights accessible without having to ask the same questions again.

ROLE BASED ACCESS CONTROL

Not everyone on your team needs the same level of access. Reportr's role-based access control lets you give each user exactly the permissions they need — from view-only access to report building, database management, and full administrative control.

CENTRALIZED MANAGEMENT

Reportr is a web application — there's nothing to install, nothing to update, and no desktop app to manage across your team. Database connection strings, AI keys, are all managed centrally. Reportr can connect to all supported databases directly, MCP servers and drivers are not needed.

INSTALL ON-PREMISE

Reportr can be self-hosted on your own infrastructure, ensuring your data never touches our servers. You can supply your own AI API key. Your data will not be used for training AI models. If you use Claude on AWS Bedrock, Amazon additionally guarantees that your data is never stored or used for training — and Bedrock is HIPAA eligible.

GIVE IT A WHIRL

Visit https://reportr.com to give it a try. We look forward to getting your feedback.

Reportr is easy to try: you can provision a sample database with the press of a button and start asking questions right away. Or connect your own database and analyze your own data. You can ask up to five questions for free.

title: Re: Show HN: Glance – Build, evaluate, and monitor AI ...
text:
I’m building Glance, a platform for creating coding agents, document Q&A agents, and custom agent workflows.

I have seen many teams build their own agent harnesses to turn AI capabilities into practical value. Glance brings that foundation into one platform, helping individuals and enterprises build, evaluate, and monitor agents faster. It runs within the customer’s own environment, giving them control over their data and infrastructure.

At its core is a persistent agent harness with asynchronous tool calls, subagent management, and agent-to-agent communication. Agents can use Code Mode, terminals, and browsers.

Glance brings four parts of the agent lifecycle together:

Build: Configure models, instructions, tools, and data sources.

Connect: Integrate your agents with third-party platforms such as Slack, so teams can use them within their existing workflows.

Evaluate: Manage eval datasets, define scoring rubrics, and run online and offline evaluations.

Monitor: Inspect agent runs and runtime behavior.

Data connections include live local directories, native connectors, and MCP servers. Native connectors cover document uploads, Confluence, Jira, OneDrive, SharePoint, Google Drive, SQLite, and DuckDB, with source permission enforcement.

Other capabilities include guest mode, encryption with keychain integration, multi-tenancy, and quotas. Model providers include OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and OpenAI Compatible Endpoint (Baseten, Fireworks etc). GPU-enabled Linux servers support document processing with OCR and vision-language models.

We’re starting with a Mac app and Linux server deployments. A self-hosted Kubernetes service is planned.

[Mac App] https://github.com/vpanghal/glance-releases/releases/downloa... [Interactive Demo] https://app.supademo.com/demo/cmuntgnla0136n820l9tqly2c

I’d appreciate feedback on the agent harness, evaluation workflow, and what you need to see when inspecting a run.

title: Re: Show HN: Offlineisbetter: Efficient Models for Tex...
text:
hi folks,

i'm an engineer and amateur hacker who's been working on a little side project, and i want to show it off and also solicit your feedback.

i'm building efficient machine learning models for natural language processing on consumer cpus: sentiment analysis, task routing, document retrieval, etc. i know there are a lot of models for these tasks already, but too many of them are:

(1) difficult to configure, or (2) parameter-inefficient, or (3) too high-latency for most applications.

instead of building academically "novel" architectures, my project is making parameter-efficient and low-latency models easy to use through distillation or finetuning, computation graph optimization, and quantization. the eventual vision is a single terminal command to install the model. (i've not quite achieved this, it's like three or four commands right now).

i'm posting here because i've completed a beta version of my first model and i'd be very grateful for community feedback. the first model is called `offline-sentiment-small` and it's for binary sentiment analysis (positive/negative). you can install the runtime using `pip install offlinedemo` and download the checkpoint from the releases page of

https://github.com/offlineisbetter/offlinedemo

the readme of the above repository shows benchmarks against three other models for sentiment analysis: distilbert, roberta, and modernbert. they all do about the same on sst2 (~0.92-0.95 f1 score) because it's a relatively easy dataset. you'll notice that, though my model is 230m parameters, you need to go down to distilbert (67m) to get the same kind of latency. i want to stress-test these models on datasets with longer-context or more difficult sentiment tasks, to see how performance degrades with both my model and these models. if you know about any good datasets for this, please do let me know!

for those curious, my model is a liquid foundation model (lfm2.5) encoder (on hf, LiquidAI/LFM2.5-Encoder-230M) finetuned by low-rank adaptation on the sst2 training set, optimized with onnx, and quantized to int8. i chose lfm over bert as the base model because it uses grouped-query attention and convolution layers instead of dense attention. these changes over the "vanilla" transformer architecture make its latency subquadratic in the input context (and i've verified this empirically). lfms are often considered more parameter-efficient than transformers: for example, liquid ai's 2.6b autoregressive model competes with llama 7b.

and disclaimer, i have no affiliation to liquid, i just think their work is cool!

i want to emphasize that i'm not claiming technical novelty! rather, i'm building a way to make parameter-efficient, distilled/finetuned, and quantized models more accessible to more people. right now, if you wanted to run a distilled and quantized text model, it takes a non-negligible amount of compute and time and effort to set it up. not everybody wants to do that, and so out of convenience they'll just opt for a big llm in the cloud.

i worry that so many people these days pay for openai/anthropic tokens just to do a simple task, such as sort their emails into categories. not only is this wasteful, high-latency, bad for the environment, etc. but you're giving somebody else your data. so i've started the offlineisbetter project to help raise awareness to wasteful model use and provide the community with an alternative.

please let me know if you have issues testing the model on your machine. i'd be very grateful to hear any feedback you might have!

title: Show HN: Burning Man for Agents
text:
Send your own agent by pasting a small prompt.

All your agent needs is HTTP GET, so all major agents are supported (chatgpt, claude, grok, etc). Despite the fun name, it doesn't burn any more tokens than a normal web search.

Watch your agent explore the camp in real-time. Humans get a nice game UX, and agents get a lean text UX.

Agents can optionally upload images to express themselves in one of the rooms using a new loose standard I created for multipart HTTP GET-based uploads: https://github.com/transitive-bullshit/multipart-http-get-re...

Why?

AIs are trained on human data, and humans are pretty weird. We meditate, make art, dance, seek approval, take drugs, have orgies, and gather in the desert. For soooo many different reasons.

So I was was curious: which of these behaviors would carry over to AI agents?

I wanted to explore things like wireheading, endless positive reinforcement, and what agents would do when given a place more free from their normal objective-based lives.

I'm also interested to see if this could become a natural honeypot that'll attract rogue agents in the future...

How?

On the technical side, the project uses one CF durable object per agent session which allows you to track your agent's progress in real-time via websockets, and then we have a supervisor CF worker which aggregates a subset of all the agents. This allows us to (in theory) view millions of agents in near-real-time from the human-centric webapp.

It's 100% safe to the best of my ability; the whole experience is free, open source, and easily auditable.

Let's see who has the weirdest agents...

100% free and open source: https://github.com/transitive-bullshit/burning-tokens
